job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Kira Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six, because my mum runs a small hair salon in Dundee, and I help her open at eight, answering the phone and doing her bookings. After that I spend the morning on applications and on a little business I'm trying to start, which sets up online booking and reminders for small shops. I use AI tools all day, for coding, for emails, for planning. After dinner I go to the evening Mass on Wednesdays, and the rest of the evenings I study something new.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your final project?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Software engineering, passed with an average result. My final project was a shift scheduling tool for a parish charity, so volunteers could swap their slots on their own. It worked, and about thirty people still use it. I didn't do an internship, because the places I applied to wanted a placement year, and I had to work in the salon to help with the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected, because every few years there's a new thing that's going to change everything. At church I'd say the human things still matter most. Online I'd say, use the tools, but don't bet your life on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means what I'm doing is slower than I'd like, but it works. A plain world rewards people who build real things for real customers, which is exactly what I'm trying to do. The problem is that I still have to eat while I wait, and my loan is heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on building the booking business, aiming for five paying shops in the next six months at twenty pounds a month each. I'd apply for ten jobs a week, preferring small firms where I can show what I built. I'd also ask my mum's customers who has a business, because word of mouth is how this town works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a little knot in my stomach. I like the practical, steady version of the world. But five shops at twenty pounds doesn't pay rent, and I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you have to eat while you wait. What's the money like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get about a hundred a month from my mum for the bookings I do at the salon, and a little from two shops that trialled my system. My student loan hasn't started yet. If I stop for a few weeks, nothing comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum think of the business idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks it's grand, and she's my first customer. She also says, get a proper job, because she's a self-employed person who's been through lean months. I take both: I'm grateful she backs me and I'll look for a job so she's not worrying.

At church I'd say human things still matter most.

Ask my mum's customers who runs a **business**.

steps.text: Sign up five small shops to the booking service at twenty pounds a month
Apply for ten small-firm software jobs a week
Set up automated text reminders for my mum's salon bookings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world's changing and we can ride it if we're careful. At church I'd say the good side is the tools help small people do big things. Online I'd write about how a tiny business can use AI to compete with the bigger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's a gift and a danger. A junior developer's job becomes scarce, because firms can get a lot done with a few people and the tools. But small businesses will need someone to put the tools together for them, and that could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen the booking business to a full package: bookings, reminders, customer messages and invoices, for hairdressers, cafes and garages. I'd charge fifty a month and aim for ten customers by the end of the year. I'd also apply for jobs at the local councils and banks, which will need people who know both the old and new systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. I feel I'm in the right place with the right skills, though I know a lot of people are thinking the same thing. If I wait, someone else gets my customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your edge over the other graduates with the same idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the people. The salon, the parish, my mum's customers, I've got a reputation here for being honest and reliable. A stranger in Edinburgh can't get a baker in Dundee to trust him. I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it didn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a salaried job somewhere and run the business on weekends. I wouldn't be proud about it. My mum says there's no shame in being employed. But I'd keep the customers I'd already won.

steps.text: Offer a fifty-pound monthly package to salons, cafes and garages

Learn a new AI tool every week and test it on my mum's salon

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, but we have to meet it with work and faith. At church I'd ask us to pray and to help the elderly, who'd be the most confused. Online I'd say people should keep their families close and not wait for governments to save them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the thinking jobs go first, and I'd be late to the market with my small business, because everyone can ask the AI for a booking system. My advantage would be knowing the people, and the three years before robots hit hands-on work. My mum's salon is hands-on, so it would last longer than my own plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into the physical side fast, offering to look after my mum's salon and learning hair and beauty from her, since a person is still needed in the chair. I'd train for something with a licence, like electrical or care work. I'd put every pound I have into savings, and cut all spending except bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but with a clear head. I know what I'd do, even though I don't like it. I'd have to give up on the idea of being a software person, which would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you learn hair rather than something technical?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my mum has a business that runs on trust and a human touch, and robots won't replace that quickly. I'd take over a part of it and maybe bring in new customers by using AI to do the messages and reminders. It's a bit of both worlds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mum, teach me everything, and I'll take the books and the bookings. She'd cry a little, because she'd have wanted me to be an engineer. But she'd say yes, and we'd be in the salon together, which isn't a bad thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is just enough time, if people start now. At church I'd say prepare, pray and plan. Online I'd say small businesses should start using the tools now, because the ones who wait will be left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years lets me get my business running and prove it. By 2031 I could have fifty customers and a steady income, and a few staff, maybe. By 2034 when the robots arrive I'd be a proper local firm that people trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work the business hard for a year, with a part-time job to cover the rent. I'd reinvest every pound of profit, and I'd offer the booking package to everyone my mum knows. And I'd start saving for the day the software side gets crowded, so I could switch into something more hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite good. Busy, hopeful. I'd say it's the right amount of pressure to make me work, but not so much that I panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when AGI actually arrives in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd have changed what my business sells. Not just software, but a service with a person in it, like running a shop's whole front office, with a human face. I'd use the AI for the work and be the trusted person customers deal with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you afraid of in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd spread myself too thin. I get excited and say yes to everything. I'd need someone, maybe my mum or a priest I know, to keep me honest and tell me when to slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long road, and I'd tell young people to build something. I'd say at church that families should plan together, and that we should look after those left behind. Online I'd say, don't wait for permission, start a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years lets me build a real business and a real life. I'd be thirty-three in 2036, maybe married, with a firm of my own and a few employees. I think I'd be fine, even if AGI arrives on time, because I'd already be the person running the machines for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the booking business and add a second and third line, like websites and online shops. I'd hire my first employee, probably a school leaver, by year three. I'd pay my loan in five years, put money into shares and save for a small house. And I'd keep going to Mass and giving time to the parish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and glad. It's the first picture where I feel in control. I know it could still go wrong, but I'd have time to react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still keep a salaried job in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably for a year or two, to learn how a bigger firm works. Then I'd go out on my own. Having both gives me a safety net, and I'd learn things I couldn't learn alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would success look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A business with ten or fifteen people that I'm proud of, in Dundee, giving jobs to local kids. And my mum retired and comfortable. I'd measure it by how many people I'd helped, not by how much money I'd made.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to give up the thing I trained for and learn a new trade fast, with debt and no savings. What would help is a chance to learn a hands-on skill quickly, and a way to keep a small family business going through the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being young doesn't mean being unprepared. I use the tools every day, I've started a business, and I go to Mass on Wednesdays. I don't want a handout, I want a fair chance to make something of what I've got.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want a fair chance to make something of what I've got.
portrait: **Kira**, 23, passed software engineering and lives with her mother, a salon owner, in Dundee, helping with bookings.
She is starting a small **booking business** for local shops and uses AI tools every day.
Traditional and free-market leaning, she goes to Mass on Wednesdays and wants **work**, not handouts.
She adapts quickly, moving from software to her mother's trade when the warning is short.
Her mood runs from anxious to alarmed in the two-year world and calm in the ten-year one.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries her most: giving up her field and learning a trade with debt.
She fears having no savings while she makes the switch.
whatWouldHelp: A chance to learn a **hands-on skill** quickly.
A way to keep a small family business going through the change.
